query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a 1–2 at.% addition of Nb (or Ti) into conventional eutectic high-entropy alloys will trigger in situ nano‐precipitation that refines the lamellar spacing, thereby concurrently enhancing dislocation pinning and promoting heterogeneous deformation. This modification is expected to yield at least a 20% improvement in both yield strength and ductility under ambient tensile conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with a coarse lamellar, dual-phase (e.g., fcc + B2) microstructure produced by standard casting processes.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a 1–2 at.% addition of Nb (or Ti) during alloy fabrication to promote controlled nano‐precipitation.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature uniaxial tensile testing conditions with otherwise identical processing parameters as the baseline alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates that refine the eutectic lamellae spacing and serve as obstacles to dislocation motion while providing heterogeneous sites for strain accommodation.
generation.mechanism: The Nb/Ti addition facilitates the formation of fine, uniformly distributed nano‐precipitates during solidification. These precipitates act as dislocation barriers (increasing strength) and also promote localized plastic deformation (increasing ductility), thereby overcoming the traditional trade-off between these properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: At least a 20% increase in both yield strength and ductility (total elongation) compared to the baseline alloy without the alloying addition.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy without the Nb/Ti addition, exhibiting a conventional coarse lamellar microstructure with typical strength–ductility trade-offs.
generation.boundary: The hypothesized improvements are expected under ambient structural loading conditions and for alloys having similar phase compositions and processing routes. Deviations in processing parameters or phase constitution may limit the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements and uniformity of nano‐precipitate formation are sensitive to precise alloy composition and cooling rates during processing, which may vary the benefits observed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA specimens: one with the standard composition and one with an added 1–2 at.% Nb (or Ti). Process both sets using identical casting and heat-treatment techniques. Conduct uniaxial tensile tests under ambient conditions and perform detailed microstructural analysis (via TEM/SEM) to verify nano‐precipitate formation and lamellar spacing.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of precipitate distribution and lamellar spacing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb/Ti-modified alloys do not exhibit at least a 20% improvement in both yield strength and ductility relative to the baseline or if the expected nano‐precipitate microstructure is not observed, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Taking into account the effect of strain rate, Li et al. conducted tensile simulations on an AlCrFeCuNi alloy and a CoNiFeAlCu alloy to study the mechanical properties of the alloys and the main mechanism of plastic deformation. The results showed that the AlCrFeCuNi alloy had not only high strength but also good plasticity. With the increase in strain, the AlCrFeCuNi alloy produced dislocation and stratification. Dislocation slip twins were the main deformation mechanism of the AlCrFeCuNi high-entropy alloy. Due to severe lattice distortion and high local strain, the CoNiFeAlCu alloy induced a phase transition from FCC to BCC. This phase transition mechanism can make the CoNiFeAlCu alloy obtain high ductility and high strength at the same time. In addition, this phase transition is mainly affected by the strain rate [,]. M-pass specimen exhibits very high yield strength (YS) of 950 MPa with a reasonable ductility of 12% in comparison with as-cast material having YS of 400 MPa and ductility of 7%. When compared with the values of YS reported by Li et al., for DP-HEA, DP-5Si-HEA showed almost 100 and ~600 MPa increase in YS for as-cast and M-pass specimens respectively. Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) for structural applications in their typical as‐cast or conventionally processed state, featuring coarse lamellar microstructures with soft and hard phases.
frame.goal: To simultaneously improve both strength and ductility relative to the baseline eutectic HEA microstructure.
frame.limitation: The inherent trade‐off between strength and ductility in eutectic HEAs, where measures to increase one often reduce the other.
constraints: intervention must be applicable to structural alloys
must yield a testable hypothesis complete with mechanism, expected improvement, conditions, supporting evidence and a falsification experiment
frame.regime: Ambient or room-temperature structural load-bearing conditions under uniaxial tension (or similar mechanical tests) used to probe both yield strength and ductility.
prior_attempts: Adjusting phase fractions or microstructural refinement through multi-step processing, which improved one property (usually strength) at the expense of the other
Dual interventions or alloying approaches where the trade-off was not satisfactorily overcome
frame.understanding: The mechanism whereby a carefully tailored nano-scale modification (e.g., in-situ nano-precipitation) can simultaneously enhance dislocation pinning (for strength) and facilitate heterogeneous deformation (for ductility) in a eutectic microstructure.
frame.method: A single compositional intervention by adding a small (~1–2 at.%) amount of a carbide‐ or intermetallic‐formers (e.g., Nb or Ti) to promote controlled nano-precipitation during solidification. The nano-precipitates would refine the eutectic spacing, serve as obstacles to dislocation motion (thereby increasing yield strength), and provide sites for strain accommodation (improving ductility). This intervention is expected to yield at least a 20% improvement in both tensile strength and elongation relative to the baseline alloy. Prior studies in multi-phase and precipitation-strengthened alloys suggest that optimized nano-precipitates can overcome the typical strength–ductility trade-off. An experiment to falsify this hypothesis would involve fabricating otherwise identical eutectic HEAs with and without the trace addition, then performing comparable mechanical tests under controlled conditions; if the alloy with the addition does not show the anticipated improvements in both properties, the hypothesis would be disproved.

families.best_lever: Introduce a small (~1–2 at.%) addition of Nb or Ti to trigger in situ nano‐precipitation that refines the eutectic spacing and serves as both obstacles to dislocation motion and sites for strain accommodation.

cues_for: enhanced heterogeneous deformation via nano-scale features
cues_against: the intervention must be achieved by a single, typically compositional, change rather than complex architectural design via processing
families.best_lever: Leveraging the formation of a refined lamellar structure through nano-precipitation induced by a trace alloying addition (which indirectly engineers the microstructure) rather than direct post-processing.
